hints: Start by remembering how ammonium is formed, ammonia plus a proton, and ask what that tells you about lone pairs and proton transfer.
Count the regions of electron density around nitrogen in $\text{NH}_4^+$, four N-H bonds and zero lone pairs, to fix its shape and hybridisation.
Think of $\text{NH}_4^+$ as the conjugate acid of ammonia and write what happens when it meets a strong base like $\text{OH}^-$.
walkthrough:
**Draw the structure of ammonium**

Think of ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, using its lone pair to form a dative bond to $\text{H}^+$. That gives $\text{NH}_4^+$. 

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$$

**Work out shape and hybridisation**

Nitrogen now has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs. Four pairs repel equally, so the shape is tetrahedral with angles about $109.5^\circ$. 

That means nitrogen uses four $\sigma$-bonds, so it is $\text{sp}^3$ hybridised, not $\text{sp}^2$.

**Check acid-base behaviour**

A Brønsted-Lowry base accepts a proton, which needs a lone pair. $\text{NH}_4^+$ has no lone pair left, so it cannot be a base. It can only donate a proton, so it acts as an acid. 

With hydroxide it is neutralised back to ammonia:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Pick the correct statement**

Only the reaction with $\text{OH}^-$ to give ammonia matches all of this logic, so that statement is correct.

options.A: Incorrect. A Brønsted-Lowry base must accept $\text{H}^+$, which requires a lone pair. $\text{NH}_4^+$ has used up the nitrogen lone pair to bond to the fourth H, so it cannot accept another proton. It is the conjugate acid, not a base. Students often confuse it with $\text{NH}_3$, which is a base.
options.B: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ acts as a weak acid and is deprotonated by strong base $\text{OH}^-$ to reform ammonia: $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. This is the classic test for ammonium salts with warm NaOH.
options.C: Incorrect. Pyramidal with $107^\circ$ describes ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, which has 3 bonds plus 1 lone pair. Ammonium, $\text{NH}_4^+$, has 4 bonds and no lone pair, so it is tetrahedral with angles of $109.5^\circ$.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{sp}^2$ is for 3 electron domains, like in trigonal planar $\text{BF}_3$. Nitrogen in $\text{NH}_4^+$ has 4 sigma bonds and 4 electron domains, so it is $\text{sp}^3$ hybridised.
